title: Exposing the Gmail “Zero-Day” Behind Remus Stealer’s Email Interception Feature
summary: How a Silently Installed Chrome Extension Gives Remus Access to Victims’ Mailboxes
body_markdown:
By[Vojtěch Krejsa](https://www.gendigital.com/blog/authors/vojtech-krejsa)


,[Jan Rubín](https://www.gendigital.com/blog/authors/jan-rubin)


## Key Points


-


On November 8, 2026, the developers behind Remus Stealer began promoting a new Gmail interception feature, promising access to victims' mailboxes independently of any stolen cookies, even after the victim changes their password and revokes all sessions.


-


The developers attribute the feature to a Gmail zero-day vulnerability they supposedly had discovered themselves, boasting of being the only ones on the market offering such a capability.


-


Gen Threat Labs has tracked down the module behind the feature and found that, rather than exploiting a Gmail vulnerability, it silently installs a malicious extension into the victim's Google Chrome browser.


-


In this blog post, we provide a technical breakdown of the malicious module and the techniques Remus uses to maintain continuous access to victims' mailboxes.


## Introduction


Imagine a Gmail vulnerability that allows threat actors to silently access victims' mailboxes independently of any stolen cookies, and to keep that access even after the victim changes their password and revokes all sessions. That is exactly what the developers of Remus Stealer began promoting on underground forums on November 8, 2026, boasting of being the only ones on the market offering such a feature and attributing it to a Gmail zero-day vulnerability they had supposedly discovered themselves. Unsurprisingly, such bold claims quickly drew attention across the security community, raising the question of whether Remus had truly found a Gmail zero-day, or whether it was all just a well-crafted sales pitch.


Figure 1: The Remus developers promoting the new Gmail interception feature on an underground forum.


The first to point out Remus' email interception feature outside underground forums was[g0njxa in a post on X](https://x.com/g0njxa/status/2119470171802714453?a=O8UwVyAGD1w6c02qB5w&s=20) , and a day later, Hudson Rock followed up with[a more in-depth investigation](https://www.hudsonrock.com/blog/remus-stealer-markets-persistent-gmail-access-hudson-rock-investigates) . As part of this investigation, they reached out to the Remus developers, who, however, revealed only that the feature works by interacting with the browser's memory, declining to disclose any further technical details to avoid "quick fixes", and, presumably, to protect what is arguably one of their product's main selling points at the moment.


Figure 2: The Remus developers’ description of the Gmail interception feature (source: Hudson Rock).


To get the other side of the story, Hudson Rock also questioned a Remus customer who had publicly endorsed the feature. When asked, the customer echoed the developers' claims, replying that mailbox access persisted even after the victim closed the browser, reset their sessions, and changed their Google password.


At this point, it is worth emphasizing that claims made by threat actors on underground forums might be far from reality, if not entirely made up, and the same goes for endorsements from their customers. Such claims should therefore always be independently verified. Hudson Rock thus rightly approached these statements with caution, concluding only that Remus most likely obtains reusable authorization from the victim's signed-in browser, while also openly acknowledging that their investigation included no technical analysis of the feature and that they could therefore neither confirm the existence of a Gmail zero-day vulnerability nor determine how the feature actually works.


Remus' bold claims have since been picked up by a number of security vendors and the media, yet the key questions remain unanswered. To the best of our knowledge, there is still no public technical analysis verifying whether Remus can really do what it promises, let alone explaining how it achieves it. In this blog post, we therefore set out to answer both, tracking down the code behind the feature and dissecting how it works under the hood.


## Technical Analysis


Before diving into the technical details, it is worth noting that, based on the publicly available information, it was not clear where the interception functionality actually resides. The feature may have been implemented directly in the malware running on the victim's machine, but it could just as easily have been handled entirely on Remus' backend, in which case there might have been no code to analyze at all (especially considering that Remus presents the feature as a zero-day vulnerability and its developers refuse to share any technical details about it). That said, the developers behind Remus did admit that the feature works by interacting with the browser's memory, which was already a strong clue that at least some part of it might run directly on the victim's machine.


Besides the email interception feature, Remus has recently introduced several other features, such as a built-in clipper, a fake Ledger, and a reverse proxy. While we will not cover them in this blog post, there is one detail worth pointing out – all of these features are advertised as standalone modules (see Figure 3). The email interceptor, on the other hand, is notably not listed as one, suggesting that it might instead be implemented directly in the core stealer binary.


Figure 3: Remus’ documentation of its features.


With that in mind, we reverse engineered the latest Remus builds, but found no trace of such functionality, suggesting that the feature is either delivered as a separate module, or handled entirely on the Remus backend. After some additional hunting, however, we eventually managed to track down the code behind the feature and found that, contrary to what the Remus documentation suggests, it is implemented as a module after all.


### Dynamic Configuration Retrieval


Rather than being embedded directly in the stealer binary, Remus' additional modules are delivered only at runtime as part of the stealer's dynamic configuration, retrieved from the C2 server. Besides the modules, this configuration also defines the stealer's collection rules, covering targeted browsers and their extensions, cryptocurrency wallets, applications, files, and registry values. As these rules can be customized by each operator, the scope of collected data may vary significantly from one operator to another, as well as across individual builds.


Importantly, this variability also applies to the stealer's modules, which is why the email interception module is only present in a subset of Remus builds. We suspect this is a consequence of Remus' tiered subscription model, with the module being reserved for the higher tiers or provided only to operators who specifically opt for the feature.


As for the retrieval, the dynamic configuration is not delivered as a single blob, but rather split into several smaller parts, which Remus downloads from the C2 server one at a time. Each of them is encrypted separately using ChaCha20, with the 32-byte key and 8-byte nonce prepended to the ciphertext. Once decrypted, each part contains one or more configuration directives in JSON format, with selected values further obfuscated using Base64 and a 4-byte XOR key stored in the first four bytes of the decoded data.


Figure 4: Visualization of the structure of Remus’ dynamic configuration.


Figure 5: Part of Remus’ dynamically retrieved configuration containing the email interception module (encoded).


Once Remus retrieves the dynamic configuration and decodes the module, it hands the module over to a newly created thread, in which it manually maps the module into the stealer's own address space and executes it from its entry point.


### Email Interception Module


In a nutshell, the loaded module is a native DLL whose sole purpose is to install a malicious extension into Google Chrome, which, notably, is the only browser it targets. The extension itself is bundled directly inside the DLL, stored as an unencrypted ZIP archive in its` .rdata` section (see Figure 6).


Figure 6: The embedded ZIP archive containing the malicious extension.


Historically, malware has commonly installed malicious extensions by launching the browser with the` --load-extension` command-line switch, either directly or through modified browser shortcuts (an approach popular mainly for its simplicity, as it required nothing more than a single command-line argument).[As of Chrome 137](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/extension-news-june-2025) , however, this switch is no longer supported in official Chrome builds. Remus therefore takes a different, considerably more complex approach, which requires several additional steps and a deeper understanding of how Chrome stores and protects its settings. Instead of relying on a command-line switch, it registers the extension directly in the victim's Chrome profile(s) by tampering with their preferences files. Registering the extension alone, however, is not enough, as additionally, starting with[Chrome 134](https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/10314655?hl=en) , unpacked extensions are only enabled while **Developer Mode** is turned on. Therefore, Remus also sets the corresponding **Developer Mode** preference.


The module's execution flow can be summarized as follows:


- Write the embedded extension archive to` %TEMP%\\<extension_id>.zip`
- Use PowerShell to extract it into` %TEMP%\\<extension_id>`


- ` powershell -command "Expand-Archive -Path '%TEMP%\\<extension_id>.zip' -DestinationPath '%TEMP%\\<extension_id>' -Force"`


- Parse` %LOCALAPPDATA%\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\Local State` and enumerate profiles under` profile.info_cache`
- For each profile, compare` %USERDOMAIN%` case-sensitively with the computer name returned by` GetComputerNameA()` and select the preferences file accordingly:


- If they are equal, select` <profile>\\Secure Preferences`
- If they differ, select` <profile>\\Preferences`


- Register the extension under` extensions.settings.<extension_id>` , including its permissions, timestamps, state, location, and installation path, and enable **Developer Mode** by setting` extensions.ui.developer_mode` to` true`
- Recompute the required` protection.macs` entries using HMAC-SHA-256 and, for the Secure Preferences branch, additionally recompute` protection.super_mac`
- Back up the original` Preferences` /` Secure Preferences` file as` <filename>.bak` in the same directory
- Attempt to terminate all running` chrome.exe` processes
- Write the modified preferences back to the selected file
- If Chrome was running, relaunch it with the` --restore-last-session` switch


Figure 7: Remus choosing between Preferences and Secure Preferences based on the %USERDOMAIN% check before patching each Chrome profile.


Figure 8: Chrome’s preferences file before (left) and after (right) Remus registers the extension, enables Developer Mode, and adds the corresponding MAC values.


So, has Remus found a novel way of getting around Chrome's preferences integrity checks to silently install browser extensions? Not at all. Based on our research, Remus only reuses a well-known technique documented as early as 2015 by[Kaimi](https://kaimi.io/2015/04/google-chrome-and-secure-preferences/) , who described how Chrome calculates the HMAC values protecting its Secure Preferences file. The technique was later analyzed in greater detail by Pablo Picazo-Sanchez, Gerardo Schneider, and Andrei Sabelfeld in their 2020 paper[HMAC and "Secure Preferences": Revisiting Chromium-based Browsers Security](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~andrei/cans20.pdf) , and more recently, in 2025, revisited by Synacktiv in their research[The Phantom Extension: Backdooring chrome through uncharted pathways](https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/the-phantom-extension-backdooring-chrome-through-uncharted-pathways) , which additionally covers domain-joined machines and the **Developer Mode** protection mentioned above. For this reason, we will not elaborate on why Remus modifies these particular JSON entries or how the corresponding MAC values are recomputed, and instead refer curious readers to the aforementioned research.


As for the extension itself, Remus disguises it as **Google Sheets** , borrowing the description word for word from the legitimate **Google Docs Offline** extension. Behind this harmless-looking facade, however, the manifest requests host permissions for all URLs (` <all_urls>` ), along with the storage and alarms permissions, and runs its logic in a background service worker (see Figure 9). To the victim, the extension simply blends in with Google's own extensions, and the only visible signs of the infection are the new extension card (marked with Chrome's unpacked icon) and the enabled **Developer Mode** switch (see Figure 10), both of which the victim will only notice if they actively check their installed extensions.


Figure 9: The malicious extension’s manifest.


Figure 10: The chrome://extensions page before (top) and after (bottom) the infection.


### Gmail Interception Browser Extension


So how does Remus supposedly manage to intercept victims' emails even after they change their password and revoke all their sessions? The answer, of course, lies in the extension's JavaScript code, which runs in a background service worker, albeit hidden behind the characteristic[obfuscator.io](https://obfuscator.io/) -style obfuscation.


Figure 11: A snippet of the extension’s obfuscated JavaScript code.


Once the obfuscation is stripped away, however, the interception mechanism turns out to be surprisingly simple, consisting of three steps that the extension repeats every minute using the alarms API:


- Discover new unread emails using Gmail's Atom feed
- Download the full messages through Gmail's attachment view
- Exfiltrate the extracted data to the C2 server


To discover new emails, the extension leverages Gmail's Atom feed (` https://mail.google.com/mail/u/<account_index>/feed/atom` ), a read-only XML feed listing the most recent unread messages in the inbox, including their senders, subjects, and short snippets of the message body.


Figure 12: An example of Gmail’s Atom feed.


Since Gmail allows up to ten accounts to be signed in at the same time within a single browser session, each identified by its index in the URL (` /u/0/` for the first account,` /u/1/` for the second, and so on), the extension queries the feed for all ten indexes. Each request is sent with credentials:` "include"` , meaning it is authenticated with the victim's existing Gmail session in the browser. From each feed, the extension then extracts the account's email address along with the IDs, senders, subjects, snippets, and dates of the unread messages.


Figure 13: The deobfuscated JavaScript code querying the Atom feed and downloading full messages.


To obtain the full content of each message (which the Atom feed provides only as a short snippet), the extension downloads the message through Gmail's attachment view endpoint (` https://mail.google.com/mail/u/<account_index>/?view=att&th=<message_id>&attid=0&disp=comp&safe=1&zw&cacheCounter=<timestamp>` ), where` <account_index>` is replaced with the index of the account the message belongs to,` <message_id>` with the message ID obtained from the Atom feed, and` <timestamp>` with the current time. This request, again authenticated with the existing session, returns the message in its raw MIME format, from which the extension parses out the headers, the plain-text or HTML body, and the names of any attachments.


Figure 14: An example of a message in its raw MIME format returned by Gmail’s attachment view.


Finally, the extension exfiltrates the subject, decoded message text, sender, and the victim's email address, along with a hardcoded campaign build ID (different from the corresponding Remus build ID), to its C2 server via an HTTPS POST request. Interestingly, while the extension records the file names of any attachments when parsing the message, it sends neither their names nor their contents to the C2 server. Messages that fail to send are queued and retried with exponential backoff, while the extension keeps track of already sent messages in` chrome.storage.local` to avoid exfiltrating the same email twice.


Figure 15: The complete interception chain of the Remus extension, from discovering new emails to their exfiltration, shown from Chrome DevTools’ point of view.


Figure 16: The Remus extension’s state stored in chrome.storage.local.


## Key Takeaways and Defensive Measures


Putting it all together, the extension by no means bypasses password changes or session revocation, nor can it be considered anything remotely close to a Gmail zero-day. Every request it makes relies on the victim's valid Gmail session, so once the sessions are revoked (or the victim simply signs out), the interception stops working as well. This is not a flaw, but simply how browser extensions are designed to work: once granted host permissions for a website, an extension can send requests to it with the user's existing cookies, just as the website itself would. After all, any malware capable of silently installing an extension could just as well steal the session cookies directly.


In other words, rather than exploiting any flaw in Gmail, what Remus really abuses is the fact that victims who change their password or revoke all sessions will most likely not notice the malicious extension still running in their browser, which eventually regains access to their new emails as soon as they sign back in.


That said, the absence of a zero-day does not make the approach any less dangerous in practice. As long as the extension remains installed, Remus can indeed intercept and exfiltrate new emails that arrive in any of the victim's signed-in Gmail accounts.
